parts.title: Who Pollinates the Flowers? The Pollinator Network and the Money Pollination Brings In Hanzhong City, China
parts.abstract:
Simple Summary

We set out to learn three things about Hanzhong City in China: which pollinators live there, how plants and insects are linked through pollination, and how much money pollination is worth to the city. Pollinators are animals, mostly insects, that carry pollen from flower to flower so that plants can make seeds and fruit. To find them, we used two methods in the field. We caught insects with nets at random spots, and we walked set routes, called transects, and counted the insects we saw along the way.

We found that Hanzhong City is rich in pollinators. We recorded 80 species of pollinators, along with 59 species of crops and wild plants that offer nectar. With so many pollinators around, local vegetables, fruits and oil crops get plenty of pollination.

The links between plants and insects formed a clear pattern. We call this pattern a pollination network. In it, each insect is connected to the plants it visits. The network had three features. It was not very tightly connected, meaning most insects did not visit every plant. It was moderately nested, meaning that insects that visit only a few plants tend to visit the same plants that busy insects visit. And it was not very specialized, meaning that most insects visit many kinds of plants rather than just one.

In 2023, the value of pollination in Hanzhong City was CNY 3524–4878 billion. That is 10.02–13.87% of the value of everything the city's farms produced that year. This share is higher than the world average.

We suggest four ways to protect pollinators in Hanzhong City: use fewer pesticides, support beekeeping, plant nectar plants among crops, and choose crops wisely.

Keywords: pollinating insects, types of habitat, pollinated crops, network of links between species, value of pollination, ways to protect pollinators
parts.introduction_first: Pollinators play an important part in nature. They carry pollen from the male parts of a flower to its female parts, which lets the flower be fertilized and produce seeds. Pollinators also help people in many ways. They let a wide variety of seeds and fruits grow. They keep wild plants alive, and those wild plants support the variety of life on Earth and the way natural systems work. They give us honey and other beekeeping products, and they matter to our cultures. Most of the world's crops and wild plants depend on animals to pollinate them [1,2].
parts.introduction_rest:
Much of the recent attention around the world on pollination has focused on how it helps us grow food. When animals pollinate crops, they directly affect how much of a crop is harvested, how good it is, or both. This is true for about 75% of the crop types that matter most around the world [3]. These include most fruits, seeds and nuts, as well as several valuable crops grown for sale, such as coffee, cocoa and oilseed rape. Without pollination, an estimated 5–8% of the world's crops would be lost. That would mean billions of dollars in lost harvests. People would have to change what they eat, and farms would have to spread over much more land to make up for the missing crops [1,2]. Many kinds of animals pollinate plants, including flies, thrips (tiny insects), beetles, birds and bats. Even so, bees are the most important pollinators for the world's crops. They visit more than 90% of the 107 leading crop types grown around the world [1,2].

China has a great variety of crops and animals. It ranks first in the world for the value of pollination, which was CNY 6790.3 billion in 2015. Much of this value is sold to markets in other countries [4,5]. China's wild pollinators are about three times as varied as Europe's. The country has 1342 species of bees [6], 125 species of bumblebees [7] (half of all bumblebee species in the world), and more than 1700 species of butterflies [8,9]. Within China, crops that depend on pollinators are often very important in a particular region. For example, in the area around Nanchong City, the value of pollination in 2023 was estimated to be at least 12.88% of the value of everything local farms produced that year [10].

The Hanzhong Plain lies between two mountain ranges, the Qinling Mountains and the Daba Mountains. Mountains, hills and plains here have created many different kinds of places for farming, and the plain has more farmland than anywhere else in Shaanxi Province. The main crops grown on the plain, where fields are farmed intensively, are oilseed rape (Brassica napus), rice (Oryza sativa) and Gastrodia elata, a type of orchid. The Qinling and Daba Mountains are a national key area for protecting nature and for the natural processes that keep the land healthy. They are also a pilot area for farming in a greener way. They are a key source of the pollinators that Hanzhong City depends on, and they are part of the plan to build model areas for farming that works with nature. In these model areas, private businesses and government departments work together. The aim is to help people understand how pollinating insects pollinate plants and how much they add to local farming. It is also to protect and make good use of these insects, so that the natural system stays healthy and stable and helps the local economy grow.

Even though pollinators are so valuable, intensive farming, where land is farmed very heavily, is still common in much of the world. There is also growing evidence that in several parts of the world, pollination is falling short in ways that cost money [11,12]. Intensive farming is common on the Hanzhong Plain, and there is little sign that it is changing. In theory, honeybees kept by beekeepers could take over the pollination that wild bees do. But China does not have enough honeybees to do this [13]. Also, more and more beekeepers in China keep their bees in one place all year instead of moving them between areas, so few beekeepers would be able to provide this kind of pollination [14].

Understanding how much pollinators are worth is thought to be key to planning good ways to manage them. But these plans need to fit a local area [15] and the needs of the most important local pollinators [16]. So far, no one has studied the important links between plants and pollinators that could support pollination on the Hanzhong Plain.

In this study, we try to fill these gaps. We looked at the pollinating insects in the Hanzhong area, at how different types of habitat affect them, and at the value of pollination. From March to September 2023, we searched for pollinator species in different habitats in Hanzhong City. These included forest, the edge where farmland meets forest, and farmland. We used four methods: catching insects at random spots, walking set routes and counting the insects we saw, collecting samples, and watching insects at fixed spots. We then worked out how the type of habitat affects pollinators and built a pollination network showing which insects pollinate which crops. We also worked out the value of pollination by insects, and we suggest ways to protect and make good use of local pollinators.
parts.methods:
## 2. What We Did and How

### 2.1. Where We Did the Study

Our study site lies in the flat farming area of Hanzhong City, in Shaanxi Province, China. It also stretches across the agroforestry ecotone, a zone where farmland meets forest. This zone runs along the southern slope of the Qinling Mountains and the northern slope of the Daba Mountains. The area lies between 105°30′ and 108°24′ east longitude and between 32°15′ and 33°56′ north latitude (Figure 1).

Figure 1

The transects we used: 5 in forested areas, 6 in agroforestry ecotones and 6 in farmland, in Hanzhong City, Shaanxi Province, China.

The climate is subtropical, which means warm and fairly wet. The average temperature over the year is 13.8 °C, and about 900 mm of rain falls each year. This warm, humid weather is a good place for pollinators to live. The land rises and falls clearly, from 1000 to 2000 m above sea level. These changes in height create many kinds of habitat, such as forests, farmland and wetlands. They also support plenty of pollinating insects, including butterflies, bees, bumblebees, hoverflies and moths. Crops in Hanzhong City that insects pollinate, such as rape, grow in long, unbroken stretches, so they give pollinators a steady supply of food [17].

### 2.2. How We Surveyed the Species

We used three methods together to learn which pollinators live here, where they are found, and which crops they pollinate. We caught insects at random spots, we kept records of what we saw, and we walked transects.

### 2.3. Choosing the Transects

We chose transects across three types of habitat: forested areas, agroforestry ecotone and farmland. When picking them, we thought about height above sea level, the shape of the land, the plants growing there and how active the butterflies were. In total we chose 17 transects, each 200 m long and 5 m wide. Five were in forested areas, 6 were in agroforestry ecotone and 6 were in farmland. Figure 1 shows where the transects are, and Figure 2 shows the three types of habitat.

Figure 2

Types of habitat in Hanzhong City: (a) forest; (b) agroforestry ecotone; (c) farmland.

### 2.4. Surveying Along the Transects

We used a well-known method called the Pollard transect survey. In this method, a person walks a set route at a steady pace and records the insects they see. We carried out the survey 6 times in Hanzhong City, from March to September 2023, with 20 days between visits. Our main focus was the variety of flowering plants and pollinating insects. Each transect was 200 m long and 5 m wide. We only surveyed on sunny days with no wind and temperatures above 16 °C.

We walked each transect at 2.5 km per hour. Along the way, we caught and recorded insects such as butterflies and bees within a strip 2.5 m wide on each side, up to 5.0 m above the ground. For each species we could identify, we noted which habitat it was in and how many individuals we saw. For species we could not identify, we caught them with nets. We kept butterflies in triangular paper bags. We put bees and hoverflies into 10 mL tubes of ethanol, a kind of alcohol that preserves insects, and took them back to the laboratory. There we prepared the specimens and identified the species.

### 2.5. Identifying the Species

To name the species, we used three reference books: the Chinese Butterfly Monography [8], the Chinese Butterfly Atlas [9], and the Tibetan Bee Atlas from the Second Comprehensive Scientific Survey of the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau [18].

### 2.6. Measuring the Variety of Pollinators

We counted how many species of pollinators there were and how many individuals of each we found. We then worked out three measures of variety, called diversity indices, using the computer programs Past 4.12 and Excel 2019. The first is the Shannon–Wiener diversity index (H′). The second is the Berger–Parker dominance index (D′). The third is the Pielou evenness index (J).

H′ measures variety by looking at how common each species is compared with the others. The higher the value, the richer the species.

D′ runs from 0 to 1. The higher the value, the more strongly one species dominates the community.

J measures how evenly the individuals are spread across the species. It also runs from 0 to 1, and the closer it is to 1, the more evenly the community is spread.

H′ = −Σ (from i = 1 to S) Pi ln Pi

Pi = Ni / N

D′ = Nmax / N

J = H′ / ln N

Here, S is the number of species in the community. Ni is the number of individuals of species i. Pi is the share of all individuals that belong to species i. N is the number of species in the community, and Nmax is the number of dominant species. The symbol Σ means "add up over all species", and ln is the natural logarithm, a standard mathematical function.

We also wanted to know whether the number of pollinating insects differed between habitats. For this we used SPSS 27 software to run a Mann–Whitney test. This is a non-parametric test, which means it does not assume the data follow a neat bell-shaped pattern. It checks whether the values in one group tend to be higher than in another. We used it to test whether there was an overall difference. If there was, we then counted how many individuals differed between the habitats.

### 2.7. Building the Pollination Network

To build the pollination network, we recorded how often different insects visited different flowering plants. We picked flowering plants at random. On each of the 17 transects, we chose flowering plants and recorded their species. We marked out a square 1 m by 1 m and watched it for 6 minutes. During that time, we noted the species of pollinators, how many there were, and how often they visited the flowers.

From these counts, we built a table with P rows and A columns, where P stands for plant species and A stands for pollinator species [19,20]. Each box in the table shows how often a pollinator visited a plant. We drew the pollination network with the bipartite package in the R programming language (version 4.3.3), which shows the pattern of links between plants and insects. We used the same package's network-level function to calculate several measures of the whole network [21,22]. These were connectance (how tightly connected the network is), links per species, the network-level specialization index (H2, how specialized the network is), weighted nestedness (how nested the network is), web asymmetry (how uneven the links are between plants and insects) and modules (groups of species that are linked mostly to each other).

### 2.8. Working Out the Value of Pollination

#### 2.8.1. How Much Do Crops Depend on Pollinators?

We started from the list of major crops closely tied to human food made by Gallai and colleagues [23]. We combined it with data from the Hanzhong Statistical Yearbook on the crop species, how much land they cover, how much they yield and how much they cost to produce. From these, we chose 11 oil crops, fruits and vegetables that are grown on a large scale and are closely tied to human food. We used them to work out the money value of insect pollination.

We estimated the value of pollination with the dependence ratio method [15]. This method treats the value of pollination as the share of a crop's production value that can be credited to pollination, within the area.

To find out how much crops depend on pollinators, we ran field experiments using gauze nets. Before the plants flowered, we chose 15–20 branches or plants and counted their flower buds. We covered them with a gauze net, hung a label on each one, and wrote on the label, with a waterproof pen, the date we covered it and the number of flower buds. After the plants flowered and formed fruit, we removed the net and counted how many flowers had turned into fruit. For comparison, we also chose 5–7 flower branches or plants, hung labels on them, but did not cover them with nets. The difference in fruiting rate between the covered and uncovered branches tells us how much the crop depends on pollinators. We carried out these experiments in Hanzhong City and in the nearby city of Nanchong [10].

#### 2.8.2. The Value of Pollination

We used the planting area and yield data for the eleven pollinated crops from the 2023 Hanzhong Agricultural Statistical Yearbook. With these, we built a model to calculate the value of pollination services.

We calculated the total economic value (PEV) of insect pollination with this formula:

PEV = Σ (from i = 1 to n) (Di × Qi × Ci)

TEV = Σ (from i = 1 to n) (Qi × Ci)

RV = PEV / TEV = [Σ (from i = 1 to n) (Di × Qi × C)] / [Σ (from i = 1 to n) (Qi × Ci)] × 100

In these formulas, i stands for the i-th pollinated crop (i ∈ [1, n]). Di is how much that crop depends on pollinating insects, from 0 to 1. Qi is the yield of the i-th crop, and Ci is the cost of producing it. TEV is the total economic output value of the pollinated crops. RV is the value of insect pollination services as a percentage of the total economic output value of the crops.

### 2.9. How We Analyzed the Data

We used SPSS Statistics 19 as our statistics program. We used the correlation function in Excel 2019 to add up the totals.
parts.results:
## 3. Results

### 3.1. How Many Kinds of Pollinators We Found

Altogether, we recorded 59 flowering plants and collected 1976 insects. These insects belonged to 80 species, 50 genera and 13 families. (A genus is a group of closely related species, and a family is a larger group of related genera.) Most of the species were butterflies and moths, which made up 58 species, or 66.59% of all the insect species we found. Next came bees, wasps and ants (the group called Hymenoptera), with 14 species, or 28.64% of the total. Flies made up the remaining 8 species, or 3.69%.

#### 3.1.1. Butterflies

We recorded 1316 butterflies from 58 species in seven families (Table 1). To compare the families, we used three measures. The Shannon–Wiener diversity index combines how many species there are with how evenly the butterflies are spread among them. A higher number means more variety. Pielou's evenness index shows how evenly the butterflies are shared out among the species. It runs from 0 to 1, and 1 means every species has the same number of individuals. The Berger–Parker dominance index shows how much one or a few species take over. It also runs from 0 to 1, and a higher number means a few species dominate.

These measures showed statistically significant differences in species diversity between the butterfly families. We call a difference statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone.

Table 1

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Papilionidae | 10 (17.24) | 408 (31.00) | 1.582 | 0.727 | 0.156 |
| Pieridae | 14 (24.13) | 536 (40.73) | 1.679 | 0.699 | 0.117 |
| Nymphalidae | 25 (43.10) | 277 (21.05) | 2.175 | 0.992 | 0.368 |
| Lycaenidae | 4 (6.89) | 45 (3.42) | 0.853 | 0.401 | 0.442 |
| Hesperiidae | 3 (5.17) | 40 (3.03) | 0.564 | 0.260 | 0.783 |
| Riodinidae | 1 (1.72) | 7 (0.53) | 0.336 | 0.470 | 0.005 |
| Danaidae | 1 (1.72) | 3 (0.23) | 0.338 | 0.770 | 0.002 |
| Total | 58 (100.00) | 1316 (100.00) | | | |

The brush-footed butterflies (Nymphalidae) had the highest Shannon–Wiener diversity index, 2.175. This reflects both their many species and their large numbers. The blues and coppers (Lycaenidae) had the highest evenness, 0.890, so their species were spread most evenly across the community. The skippers (Hesperiidae) had only three species, yet their dominance index was as high as 0.783. This shows that they were very numerous and held a leading place in the community.

The butterflies in Hanzhong City were arranged in a core–periphery pattern, with a few main groups and a few smaller ones around them. The brush-footed butterflies, whites and yellows (Pieridae) and swallowtails (Papilionidae) formed the core, with the most species and the most individuals. The blues and coppers and the skippers played a supporting role. The clearwings (Riodinidae) and the milkweed butterflies (Danaidae) were rare.

#### 3.1.2. Bees

We recorded 579 bees from 15 species in three families and six genera (Table 2). Almost all of them were honeybees: 562 bees, or 99.30% of all the bees we counted. The remaining bees were 2.41% mason bees (Megachilidae) and 0.52% paper wasps (Vespidae). The honeybee was a dominant species.

We recorded 73 flies from five genera. We also recorded eight hawk moths of the genus Macroglossum (Table 3).

### 3.2. Pollinators in Different Habitats

Our survey showed statistically significant differences between habitats in Hanzhong City. The habitats differed in how many pollinator species they held, how many individuals they held, and what their communities were like. The Shannon–Wiener diversity index was highest in the agroforestry habitat, where trees are grown among crops. This shows that the habitat is effective at supporting a wide range of pollinators. The forest habitat offers better places for pollinators to live, while the farmland habitat offers plenty of nectar. The dominance index was highest in the forest habitat, which shows that some species there were very numerous (Table 4).

Table 4

The pollinators we found in each habitat of Hanzhong City, with their diversity measures. The abundance index (R) is the number of individuals divided by the number of species.

| Habitat Type | Number of Families | Number of Genera | Number of Individuals | Abundance Index (R) | Shannon–Wiener Diversity Index (H′) | Pielou's Evenness Index (J) | Dominance Index (D) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| farmland | 6 | 23 | 591 | 4.111 | 2.598 | 0.730 | 0.175 |
| forest area | 6 | 17 | 335 | 3.491 | 2.344 | 0.911 | 0.192 |
| agroforestry | 8 | 28 | 499 | 6.811 | 3.102 | 0.839 | 0.162 |

To compare habitats, we used a non-parametric test, the Mann–Whitney test. It compares two groups by ranking their values from lowest to highest, so it does not assume the data follow a bell-shaped curve. It gives two numbers, U and z, and a p-value. We call a difference statistically significant when p is below 0.05. That means that if there were really no difference, a gap this large would appear by chance less than 5% of the time.

The test showed that habitat type had a statistically significant effect on the species diversity and abundance of pollinators (p = 0.046, below 0.05). In particular, the median estimated abundance of pollinators on farmland was 96.000, significantly higher than the 60.000 in the forest area (U = 3, z = −2.402, p = 0.016, below 0.05). This may be because farmers grow crops such as rapeseed and citrus on the farmland, which gives pollinators plenty of food and places to live. However, growing several crops together and spraying pesticides lead to low diversity.

In contrast, the number of pollinators in the agroforestry habitat was not significantly different from the number on farmland (U = 13, z = −0.8, p = 0.423, above 0.05). Nor was it significantly different from the number in the forest area (U = 8, z = −1.607, p = 0.108, above 0.05). This means we could not show a difference, not that there is none. It shows that the agroforestry habitat did not stand out from the other two habitats in how many pollinators it held (Table 5).

### 3.3. The Pollinator Network

#### (1) Which pollinators and plants were in the network

The pollination network of Hanzhong City covered 58 pollinators and 55 flowering plants. There were 252 links between insects and flowering plants. Counting every possible link between these species, that is 3190, so the links we found made up 7.9% of all possible links. This shows that the links between species are complex.

The network was not very balanced. Its asymmetry was 0.045, and there were fewer flowering plant species than pollinator species. Pollinators also had more links on average. Together, these show that pollinators have a large potential to help plants, and that they tend to visit many kinds of plants.

Next we looked at the shape of the network. It had one compartment, meaning it was not split into separate clusters. Its nestedness index was 0.5152, greater than the index of 0.4806. Its weighted nestedness was also 0.5152, close to 1. This shows that the pollination network had a nested structure.

Figure 3 shows this in a grid of colored boxes, called an interaction matrix. Each box shows whether a pollinator visits a plant. Red boxes mark seven modules, which are groups of species that interact mostly with each other, and they show the nested structure inside the network. The blue areas show the links between species, and the deeper the color, the stronger the link.

Figure 3

The interaction matrix of the pollination network in Hanzhong City, showing its modules.

To check whether the nested structure was significant, we ran 1000 simulations. We used the null model function in the bipartite package in the R software (version 4.3.3). A null model builds many random networks with the same number of species and links, so we can see how often a pattern this strong turns up by chance. The p-value of the null model network was 0.622, so the nestedness index did not reach a significant level.

Even so, our analysis of the network's features still shows that the pollination network in Hanzhong City is made of modules, with a nested structure inside each module. This network is highly modular and not very tightly connected. That helps keep the community's food web stable, and it is a two-way network that supports the steady running of the ecosystem (see Figure 3). The data are in Appendix A, Table A1 and Table A2.

#### (2) Links between insects and plants

Among the butterflies, the cabbage white (Pieris rapae) visited the most flowering plants, 16 species, which is 29.1% of all the flowering plants in the network. Next came the Asian swallowtail (Papilio xuthus), which visited 13 plants (23.6% of all plants), and the dark clouded yellow (Colias fieldii), which visited 12 (21.8%) (Figure 4).

Figure 4

The network of links between plants and insects in Hanzhong City. The size of each rectangle shows how common that species is. Magenta rectangles are pollinators, and violet-red rectangles are flowering plants (species codes are in Table A1 and Table A2). The width of each line shows how strong the link is.

The two honeybees, Apis cerana and Apis mellifera, were the most important bees. Apis cerana visited 18 flowering plant species, or 32.7% of all the plants, and Apis mellifera visited 14, or 25.5%. They visited many kinds of nectar plants and also visited them often (Figure 4).

Bumblebees were especially important for pollination. The 12 bumblebee species together visited 42 flowering plant species, which is 69.1% of all the plants. Flies and other insects visited 14 plant species, or 25.5% of all the plants, and played a supporting role in pollination.

Different flowering plants in the Hanzhong City network were visited by very different numbers of pollinators. Rapeseed (Brassica napus) had 24 pollinators, which is 41.37% of all the pollinators in the network, so it ranked first of all the plants. Bush vetch (Vicia sepium) was visited by 20 pollinators, and white clover (Trifolium repens) by 17. In addition, plants that flower for a long time, such as butterfly bush (Buddleja davidii), zinnia (Zinnia elegans), daisy fleawort (Erigeron annuus), radish (Raphanus sativus) and Chinese milkvetch (Astragalus sinicus), were each visited by more than 10 pollinators.

We also measured how strongly each plant was linked to pollinators, which we call its species strength. Of the 55 flowering plants, 18 had a species strength greater than one. Six of these were crops: rapeseed, spring onion, kale, citrus, broad bean, sesame and loofah. Each of these crops had at least two or three pollinators. This shows that these crops can make good use of local pollinators to get pollinated and produce seeds.

The pollination network in Hanzhong City was not very tightly connected and had a nested structure. Most flowering plants and pollinators visited many kinds of partners. This network structure helps keep the community stable. It is worth noting that bees hold an important place in the pollination network. Developing and protecting bees is very important for keeping the region's ecosystems stable and for farming that can last into the future. We urge the relevant government departments and researchers to pay attention to this.

#### (3) The money value of pollination

We worked out the value of pollination for 11 major pollinated crops in Hanzhong City. To do this, we used four pieces of information for 2023: the value of everything the city's farms produced, how much of each crop was harvested, its market price, and how much it depends on pollinators. From these we calculated two things. The first is the value of pollination (PVE), the money that pollinators bring in for a crop. The second is the economic contribution rate (RV), the share of the crop's value that comes from pollination.

In 2023, the value of everything Hanzhong City's farms produced was 35.2 billion CNY. The value of pollination for these 11 major crops was about 3524–4878 billion CNY. That is 10.0–13.87% of the total value of these crops. Rapeseed contributed the most, 32.4–45.1 million CNY.

Vegetable crops brought in about 155.8–173.2 million CNY from pollination, which is 4.43–4.92% of the value of everything the city's farms produced. Fruit crops brought in 164.2–278.1 million CNY, which is 4.667–7.91% of that total. Of the three types of crops, fruit crops had the highest economic contribution rate (Table 6).

Table 6

The value of insect pollination for major crops in Hanzhong City in 2023, and each crop's share of the value of everything the city's farms produced.

| Crop | Dependence on Pollinators (D) | Harvest (tons) | Price (CNY/kg) | Value of Pollination (CNY, in units of 10,000) | Economic Contribution Rate (%) |

## 4. Discussion: What Our Results Mean

In this study, we looked at the pollination network in Hanzhong City, China, a region that matters a great deal for farming. We also worked out how much money pollination is worth there. Our goal was to give local people clear advice on how to protect pollinators and how to plan future research. Our findings point to five main messages.

### (1) Hanzhong City is rich in pollinating insects

We found 80 species of pollinating insects in Hanzhong City. They belong to 13 families and 50 genera. (A genus is a group of closely related species, and a family is a larger group of related genera.) Most of these insects were butterflies, bees and flies. With so many pollinators around, local crops get plenty of pollination.

Among the butterflies, two families stood out: the brush-footed butterflies (Nymphalidae) and the whites and yellows (Pieridae). Both had many species. As we expected, bees (the family Apidae) were the insects that visited the most plants, especially crop plants. Some of these plants could also produce a lot of honey. This matches earlier studies showing that bees play a key role as pollinators across China and in pollinating crops more widely [16].

Our study is broad, but it does not cover every type of habitat or every crop in the area. Even so, it can serve as a starting point for planning how farming can grow in a way that can last.

### (2) The groups of pollinators differed clearly between types of habitat

Like earlier studies [24], we found that the groups of pollinators living in each of the three types of habitat we surveyed were different. In the more intensively managed places, where there were few kinds of plants and crops, we found fewer pollinator species and fewer individual pollinators. The agroforestry ecotone, by contrast, stood out among the three habitats. This is a border zone where trees and farming meet, and it had a very wide variety of plants and pollinators.

This is one of the first studies of pollinators in Chinese agroforestry, and in agroforestry more widely in the subtropical region. Agroforestry means growing trees together with crops or animals on the same land. Our finding fits with research from agroforestry in temperate and tropical regions. In those places, the many kinds of flowers and nesting spots in these mixed systems support a wider variety of plants and insects, and they provide more of the benefits that nature gives people [25,26].

### (3) The pollination network in Hanzhong City is highly nested

The pollination network in Hanzhong City is highly nested. It also has low compartmentality, which means it is not split into separate clusters of species that mostly link to each other. Together, these features reflect the fact that the links between species are uneven: some insects visit many plants, while others visit only a few.

Two measures show that the network is highly generalized, meaning that most insects visit many kinds of plants. The first is connectivity, which tells us how many of all the possible links between insects and plants actually exist. The second is the average number of species each insect is connected to. A network like this is likely to hold up well against outside disturbances. That is good news for keeping the natural system stable [27].

Still, our study did not cover every type of habitat in the landscape. So it may have missed some specialist plants, which depend on just one or a few kinds of pollinators. It may also have missed some damage to the network that has already happened [28]. Watching plants, pollinators and their links over many years would give a clearer picture of how much pollination, and the wider variety of life, are affected.

### (4) Pollination is worth a lot of money in the Hanzhong City region

In 2023, we estimated that pollination was worth CNY 48.8–352.9 million for 11 major pollinated crops in Hanzhong City. That is 10.02–13.87% of the value of everything the city's farms produced that year. Fruit and vegetable crops had a higher value of pollination. Pollination made up 4.67–7.90% of the value of fruit crops and 4.43–4.92% of the value of vegetable crops.

This figure only counts the money that goes to farmers. It does not include the full value of pollination to shoppers and others in the food chain [15]. That total may be much higher, because pollination adds value at each step as food is grown, processed and sold [29]. Our analysis also assumes that pollination is already happening at its highest possible level. In reality, some of this value may already be lost because pollination is falling short of what it could be, as has been seen in other parts of the world [30]. Farming is very important to the local economy, so watching over and protecting pollinators is likely to bring a large economic benefit to the community.

### (5) Our advice for protecting pollinators in Hanzhong City

①

Support beekeeping: Hanzhong City has plenty of nectar plants, such as rape, milk vetch and vitex. Supporting beekeeping can give honey and other beekeeping products, such as propolis, beeswax and royal jelly. It can also increase pollination of crops, improve food production and help wild plants reproduce. However, care is needed so that wild pollinators and honeybees do not compete too much with each other [31].

②

Plant nectar plants among crops: Citrus, apple and pear orchards depend heavily on pollinators. Planting flowers such as Brassica napus (rapeseed), Astragalus sinicus (Chinese milkvetch) and Vicia sepiu (a kind of pea) can attract bees to collect honey. Having more bees helps the orchard flowers get pollinated.

③

Encourage green farming, speed up the growth of local specialty industries, adjust methods to fit local conditions, and grow crops wisely.

Strengthen the farming systems that already mix different kinds of land use, such as forest gardens, family gardens and agroforestry. These can give pollinators a steadier supply of food and places to live. We also recommend the following. Work directly with farmers and others who are interested to spread the word about pollinators and pollination, using methods that science or local traditional knowledge has shown to work (such as crop rotation, which means changing which crop is grown in a field from season to season). Improve the natural features that pollinators need, including patches of partly wild habitat spread across farmland, and provide flowers for them. Look after green spaces in towns and in places where people relax, so that more flowering plants that offer nectar and pollen grow nearby. And increase the variety and numbers of pollinators.
